title: Moss and the Wobbly Lanterns
markdown:
The last sliver of sun, like a bright orange peel, dipped behind the pointy tops of Ferncrown. Moss’s favourite time. He was a young elf who lived in the quiet hidden terraces. Evenings meant soft twinkling lights and Hoot, his pet owl, feathers the colour of the sky as it got dark, eyes like shiny black buttons that seemed to understand, especially when Moss was full of questions or about to do something a little bit naughty.

Tonight the air felt different. A whisper of strangeness on the breeze. The usual dance of lantern ribbons—green, blue, purple loops to show the way through misty terraces—seemed wobbly. Hair like spun moonlight, Moss pointed. “Hoot, look!”

Hoot blinked. A soft questioning Hoo. Some ribbons gone, lanterns bare and lonely. Others in crooked shaky knots that might fall any second. A shiver of confusion, not cold. A puzzle at home. Moss, always-thinking, felt he was just the elf to solve it.

“We must go look!” Tummy flip-flop. Hoot ruffled, tiny knowing nod. Elf boots hardly a sound on mossy paths. Cool air, damp earth after rain, night-blooming jasmine, white petals like sleepy stars.

Around a corner, past big ferns: a funny pile of mushrooms stacked like speckled bowling pins, each wobbling on the one below. A plump toadstool on a tall skinny one on a wide flat cap. “That’s strange. Very strange.” Moss knew mushroom families. He’d never seen anyone stack them like this. As if a giant clumsy hand had dropped them.

Near glowing moss, quiet voices. Glow-worms huddled, lights like shy candles. “We saw a shadow. A very, very big shadow, moving through the terraces. Enormous!”

A flutter in Moss’s chest. Big shadows usually belonged to bigger, sometimes grumpier, creatures than elves. Hoot nudged with a wing. Comforting Hoo. Old Willow-whisper, wisest tree in Ferncrown, always said: when things seem strange, look with your heart, not just your eyes. Moss breathed jasmine.

Hoot led toward a soft steady humming: beehives in a sunny clearing past whispering pines. The ogre beekeeper lived here, a kind giant who loved buzzing bees and even bigger honey pots. As big as a mountain, beard like tangled moss, hands as big as teacups, usually yellow with pollen. Laugh a boom that shook dew off leaves. Heart warm as golden honey. Maris.

They saw Maris on tiptoes, huge body stretching toward a high branch where a ribbon would not stay tied. Enormous fingers, usually so gentle with bees, fumbled the delicate silk. A flash of blue. A stumble. Heavy boots crunched mushrooms scattered at those feet. The stacked mushrooms. It all made clumsy sense. Not naughty. Trying to fix the ribbons, huge and fiddly.

A sigh like wind in a deep cave. “Oh, fiddlesticks and flapdoodle!” Shoulders drooped.

Moss stepped forward, small voice surprisingly strong. “Excuse me, Mr. Maris?”

Maris jumped. Eyes like two giant saucers. “Ho! A little elf! And a wise-looking owl! Bless my buzzing bees! Did you get lost on your way to the berry patch?”

“We saw the lantern ribbons. And the mushrooms. It looks like you’ve been trying to help make things bright.”

A faint pink on mossy cheeks, a giant strawberry. “Aye. I always like to help make things pretty. But these ribbons are so fiddly. So slippy. And the mushrooms—I thought I’d make a little pattern while I waited for the nectar to be just right. A bit of decoration.” A huge pollen-dusted wave.

Hoot’s knowing hoot. Moss giggled. “We can help. Hoot and I are very good at tying knots. If you hold the ladder steady, we can reach those high branches.” Hoot blinked agreement.

Sunshine through clouds. “You would? Oh, that would be grand! Simply grand!” Booming happy laugh.

Maris’s giant hands held a sturdy moss-covered branch as a ladder. Moss, quick and nimble, moonlit hair a blur, tied perfect shimmering loops of green and purple. Hoot’s sharp eyes guided the tricky knots, soft hoots like little instructions. Maris gathered scattered mushrooms and, following Moss’s ideas and a good heart, arranged them in pretty colourful bunches at the lanterns’ feet: earthy jewels, cheerful stepping stones.

Soon the terraces twinkled. Ribbons danced in the soft night breeze, brighter than ever. Mushrooms in charming groups. Maris’s laugh shook the leaves. “We did it! Together!”

Warmth like the best honey. Not a strange troublemaker: a kind, if clumsy, helper, promising a pot of clover honey the next day. Moss looked up at Hoot. The lanterns, which had seemed sad and wobbly, shimmered. Evening glowed. They walked the marked way home, and Hoot, for once, did not need to say hoo. The knots held.
